## Proof

**Answer: Yes, such a matrix $B$ always exists.**

In fact, a stronger statement holds: there exists $B$ with $b_{ij} > a_{ij}$ for **every** $i,j$ (strict inequality everywhere) and all eigenvalues of $B$ strictly inside the unit circle.

**Setup.** Since $A$ is strictly positive ($a_{ij}>0$) and all its eigenvalues lie strictly inside the unit circle, the Perron–Frobenius theorem applies: the spectral radius $\rho(A)$ equals the unique positive eigenvalue of $A$ (the Perron root), and by hypothesis
$$\rho(A) < 1.$$

**Construction.** Choose any $\varepsilon$ with
$$0 < \varepsilon < \frac{1}{\rho(A)} - 1,$$
which is possible because $\rho(A) < 1$ makes the right-hand side strictly positive. Define
$$B := (1+\varepsilon)\,A.$$

**Verification of entrywise dominance.** Since every $a_{ij} > 0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$,
$$b_{ij} = (1+\varepsilon)\,a_{ij} > a_{ij} \quad \text{for all } i,j,$$
so in particular $b_{ij} \ge a_{ij}$ (indeed strictly).

**Verification of the spectral condition.** The eigenvalues of $B = (1+\varepsilon)A$ are exactly $(1+\varepsilon)\lambda$ where $\lambda$ ranges over the eigenvalues of $A$. Hence
$$\rho(B) = (1+\varepsilon)\,\rho(A).$$
By the choice of $\varepsilon$,
$$\rho(B) = (1+\varepsilon)\rho(A) < 1.$$
Therefore every eigenvalue of $B$ has modulus strictly less than $1$, i.e. all eigenvalues of $B$ lie strictly inside the unit circle.

**Conclusion.** For every strictly positive matrix $A$ whose eigenvalues are all strictly inside the unit circle, the matrix $B = (1+\varepsilon)A$ — with any $0 < \varepsilon < 1/\rho(A) - 1$ — satisfies $b_{ij} > a_{ij} \ge a_{ij}$ for all $i,j$ and has all eigenvalues strictly inside the unit circle. Hence such a $B$ always exists. $\blacksquare$
